KEY MESSAGE 1...

All eyes remain focused on a developing coastal low that will
likely usher in our first accumulating wet snow of the season
tomorrow into Friday. Latest water vapor imagery shows a potent
shortwave tracking through the Midwest and rounding the base of
broad troughing developing over southern Canada. Heights fall
ahead of the shortwave and developing sfc low as it continues 
to track into the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic tonight into 
early tomorrow. Increasing forcing for ascent and strengthening 
warm air and moisture advection looks to quickly expand into 
the Northeast including eastern NY and western New England by 06
to 12 UTC tonight allowing mainly rain to begin. The higher 
terrain of the western Adirondacks should be cool enough that
p-type favors rain/snow mix initially before becoming mainly wet
snow. Steady rain continues across the region, especially along
and north of I-90 where the stronger warm air/moisture 
advection resides, through tomorrow morning making for a wet
Thursday morning commute. The ongoing rain will keep
temperatures cool from wet-bulinb/diabatic cooling effects with
most staying in the 30s and 40s through the day. The southern
Adirondacks will remain wet snow through the day with even the
foothills becoming a rain/snow mix given cooling temperatures.
Elevations at and above 1500ft in southern VT and the 
northern/eastern Catskills will eventually succumb to the 
cooling temperatures with rain becoming a rain/snow mix by the 
afternoon and the spine of the Greens becoming mainly wet snow.

Our sfc low deepens further as it reaches the mid-Atlantic/southern
New England coast and undergoes cyclogenesis by Friday evening 
as the shortwave takes on a negative tilt. North-northeast winds
on the north side of the low will support cool air advection 
into eastern NY and western New England Friday night. Mid-level 
frontogenesis looks to support mesoscale banding on the
northwest side of the storm which should support periods of
moderate precipitation overnight. There remains uncertainty 
regarding the exact storm track which will be important in the 
placement of the developing mesoscale bands. Latest trends track
the low a bit further south which would place the bands mainly 
from the eastern Catskills north and east into southern VT but 
this is only a low to moderate confidence in the exact 
placement. Where these bands form will have higher potential for
heavy enough precipitation to occur that diabatic cooling 
effects can allow temperatures to cool towards their respective 
wet-bulb temperatures and support a changeover to wet snow. 
Latest forecast soundings continue to show cool air advection 
from breezy northerly winds combining with diabatic cooling 
effects that thermal profiles even in valley areas from the 
Capital District northward support a changeover to wet- snow 
mainly 06 - 12 UTC Friday. While surface temperatures will be 
marginal only in the low to mid-30s, where any mesoscale bands 
that can result in moderate/heavy precipitation rates will have 
the highest chance for wet snow to accumulate. Given rather warm
ground surfaces and a lack of an antecedent cool air mass, any 
wet snow accumulations in the valley will likely be limited to 
grassy/cooler sfcs with roads likely remaining wet. Our latest 
forecast continues to show a few tenths of snow in the valley to
help message this potential with NBM probabilistic guidance 
showing a 25 to 40% chance of at least 0.1" of snow through 
early Friday morning.

Higher terrain areas including the southern Greens, northern/eastern
Catskills, Helderbergs, western MA, Taconics, western/southern 
Adirondacks have the highest chance for accumulating wet snow 
with the latest NBM probabilistic guidance showing a 40 to 80% 
chance for at least 2 inches of snow and a 30 to 60% chance for 
at least 4 inches in the 24 hr period ending 7am Friday. The
latest probabilistic WSSI values have also trended upwards for
"minor impacts" with values now ranging 20 to 40% with even
isolated pockets of 50% in the southern Greens/eastern
Catskills. Given these trends and slight increase in wet snowfall
amounts, we issued the first Winter Weather Advisories of the
season for the southern Adirondacks, southern Greens, and
eastern Catskill from Thursday into Friday morning where amounts
range 2 to 5 inches. While these amounts are on the low end of
our advisory criteria, we erred on the side of caution and went
with the advisory given wet snow character that can lead to
isolated power outages, this being the first event of the 
season and potential slippery travel for the Friday morning 
commute. We also show 1 to 3 inches of wet snow in the 
Helderbergs, higher terrain of western MA into the Rensselaer 
Plateau. The recent southerly shift in the storm track would 
favor any mesoscale banding placement in the eastern Catskills
